title: What are the Golden Signals of monitoring (latency, traffic, errors, saturation)?
shortTitle: The Golden Signals of monitoring (latency, traffic, errors, saturation)

s1_definition.profdef: The Golden Signals are the four metrics that, taken together, give the most complete picture of a user-facing system's health: latency, the time taken to serve a request, measured separately for successes and failures; traffic, the demand on the system such as requests per second; errors, the rate of requests that fail explicitly, implicitly, or by policy; and saturation, how full the system's most constrained resource is relative to its capacity. If you can only monitor four things on a service, these are the four, because together they tell you whether users are being served well and whether the system is heading toward trouble.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a teller counter at the National Bank of India serving Rajesh, Priya, and everyone else. Latency is how long each customer waits at the counter to be served. Traffic is how many customers arrive per minute. Errors is how many customers leave without their transaction done — rejected or failed. Saturation is how full the counter's capacity is: are all the tellers busy, is the queue overflowing, is the cash drawer nearly empty. Watch those four and you know almost everything: are customers served quickly, how busy is it, are things failing, and are we about to run out of capacity.
s1_definition.oneliner: Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation are the four Golden Signals — serve-time, demand, failure rate, and how-full — and together they tell you nearly everything about a user-facing service.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Golden Signals are the four metrics that, taken together, give the most complete picture of a user-facing system's health: latency, the time taken to serve a request, measured separately for successes and failures; traffic, the demand on the system such as requests per second; errors, the rate of requests that fail explicitly, implicitly, or by policy; and saturation, how full the system's most constrained resource is relative to its capacity. If you can only monitor four things on a service, these are the four, because together they tell you whether users are being served well and whether the system is heading toward trouble.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a teller counter at the National Bank of India serving Rajesh, Priya, and everyone else. Latency is how long each customer waits at the counter to be served. Traffic is how many customers arrive per minute. Errors is how many customers leave without their transaction done — rejected or failed. Saturation is how full the counter's capacity is: are all the tellers busy, is the queue overflowing, is the cash drawer nearly empty. Watch those four and you know almost everything: are customers served quickly, how busy is it, are things failing, and are we about to run out of capacity.

**One line to remember:** Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation are the four Golden Signals — serve-time, demand, failure rate, and how-full — and together they tell you nearly everything about a user-facing service.

sections.s2_technical:
Latency is how long a request takes. The critical refinement is that you must separate the latency of successful requests from the latency of failed ones, because a fast error is still a failure and mixing them hides problems — a flood of fast 500 errors could otherwise make your latency graph look great. You measure latency as percentiles, not averages, because the average hides the slow tail that real users feel; p50, p95, and p99 together show the typical and the worst-case experience. Rising latency is often the earliest warning that a system is struggling before it starts erroring.

Traffic measures the demand on the system — for a web service it is requests per second, for a streaming system it might be bytes per second, for a database it might be transactions or queries per second. Traffic is the context for everything else: a spike in errors during a traffic surge tells a different story than the same error spike during normal traffic. Traffic also drives capacity planning, and a sudden drop in traffic can itself be a symptom, for example an upstream failure that stops requests reaching you.

Errors is the rate of failed requests. These come in three flavours. Explicit errors are obvious, like an HTTP 500. Implicit errors are responses that look successful but are wrong, like an HTTP 200 that returned the wrong content or an empty result that should have had data. Policy errors are responses that are technically fine but violate a requirement, such as a response that took longer than your latency SLO and so counts as failed for budget purposes. A good error signal captures all three, which often requires measuring from the client's perspective, not just the server's status code.

Saturation measures how full the system is, focusing on the most constrained resource — the one that will run out first. For a CPU-bound service it is CPU utilization; for a memory-bound one it is memory; for a database it might be connection pool usage or disk IOPS; for a queue it is queue depth and how fast it is draining. Saturation is forward-looking: it predicts near-future problems, because systems usually degrade as they approach full capacity, and latency often rises sharply once saturation passes a threshold like eighty percent. You also watch the rate of change — a resource climbing steadily toward full gives you time to react.

The signals work together, which is their real value. A senior nuance: the Golden Signals are a focused subset deliberately chosen over the hundreds of metrics a system can emit, so you alert on these four at the user-facing level and keep the deeper resource metrics for diagnosis once an alert fires. They map cleanly onto SLIs — latency and errors are your primary user-facing SLIs, traffic gives context, and saturation is your leading indicator for capacity. The USE method (utilization, saturation, errors) is a related resource-centric view, while the Golden Signals are more request-centric; mature teams use both, the Golden Signals for the service and USE for the underlying resources.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's transfer service needs a single health view built on the four Golden Signals so the on-call engineer sees everything that matters at a glance.

Problem 1 — The service must separately measure the latency of successful transfers and failed transfers, because a burst of fast failures must not disguise itself as low latency. This is the latency signal done correctly.

Problem 2 — The service must report traffic as transfers per second to give context, and errors as the rate of failed transfers including both explicit failures and policy failures where a transfer exceeded the latency target.

Problem 3 — The service must report saturation as the usage of its most constrained resource, the database connection pool, because that is what runs out first under load for transfers between Rajesh, Priya, and other customers.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `GoldenSignals` collector that records each transfer with its outcome and latency, tracks pool usage, and reports latency percentiles split by outcome, traffic, error rate, and saturation, with a `SignalDashboard` that classifies overall health. Classes: `GoldenSignals`, `SignalDashboard`, and a `GoldenSignalsDemo` main.

```bash

java -cp target/classes com.bank.monitor.GoldenSignalsDemo

# Real Golden Signals in Prometheus:
#   LATENCY : histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le)(rate(transfer_duration_seconds_bucket{outcome="success"}[5m])))
#   TRAFFIC : sum(rate(transfers_total[1m]))
#   ERRORS  : sum(rate(transfers_total{status="failure"}[5m])) / sum(rate(transfers_total[5m]))
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a ten-second window of transfer traffic with a database connection pool of fifty, containing nine hundred fast successes, ninety slow successes as the pool saturates, and sixty fast failures when the pool is exhausted.

Step 1: The collector records the nine hundred fast successful transfers, each around forty to a hundred milliseconds, at low pool usage. The success latency list fills with fast values, traffic accumulates, and errors stay at zero.

Step 2: As demand rises, the pool usage climbs toward its capacity of fifty. Ninety more successful transfers are recorded but now take over five hundred milliseconds because they wait for a free connection. These slow successes push the success p99 upward.

Step 3: The pool reaches full. Sixty transfers are rejected immediately because no connection is available, each failing in about eight milliseconds. These are fast failures, but they are still errors — recorded in the failure latency list and the error count, not the success latency. This is why separating success and failure latency matters: the fast rejects do not make the latency graph look healthy.

Step 4: The dashboard reports all four signals. Success p99 is high, traffic is about a hundred and five transfers per second, the error rate is around six percent, and saturation is a hundred percent because the pool filled. The combined verdict flags errors above one percent, slow success latency, and saturation over eighty percent.

Step 5: Reading the four together tells the whole story: saturation of the connection pool was the root cause, which produced fast-reject errors and simultaneously slowed the successful transfers. No single signal alone would have revealed the full picture.

```
2026-10-30 02:45:30 [INFO   ] National Bank of India — Golden Signals dashboard for transfer service
2026-10-30 02:45:30 [INFO   ] LATENCY : p99 success=598ms, p99 failure=8ms (separated so fast errors don't hide)
2026-10-30 02:45:30 [INFO   ] TRAFFIC : 105.0 transfers/sec
2026-10-30 02:45:30 [INFO   ] ERRORS  : 5.71% of transfers failed
2026-10-30 02:45:30 [INFO   ] SATURATE: DB pool 100.0% full
2026-10-30 02:45:30 [SEVERE ] HEALTH: ERRORS above 1% — users impacted, investigate now
2026-10-30 02:45:30 [WARNING] HEALTH: success p99 > 500ms — slow for users even when working
2026-10-30 02:45:30 [WARNING] HEALTH: saturation > 80% — capacity running out, scale soon (leading signal)
2026-10-30 02:45:30 [INFO   ] Read together: SATURATION (pool full) caused ERRORS (fast rejects) and pushed success LATENCY up — all visible via the four signals.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Golden Signals are the four metrics that together give the most complete picture of a user-facing service's health: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. If I could only monitor four things on a service, these are the four. Latency is how long a request takes, and the critical refinement is that I measure the latency of successful requests separately from failed ones, because a fast error is still a failure, and if I mixed them a flood of fast 500s could make my latency graph look deceptively healthy. I always measure latency as percentiles rather than averages, because the average hides the slow tail that real users actually feel.

Traffic is the demand on the system, usually requests per second, and it is the context for everything else — the same error spike means something very different during a traffic surge than during normal load, and traffic drives capacity planning. Errors is the rate of failed requests, and I capture all three kinds: explicit errors like an HTTP 500, implicit errors where a 200 response is actually wrong or empty, and policy errors where a response was technically fine but violated a requirement such as exceeding the latency SLO. Saturation is how full the most constrained resource is — the one that runs out first, like a database connection pool or CPU — and it is the leading indicator, because systems degrade as they approach full and latency usually rises sharply past about eighty percent utilization.

The real value is reading them together. In my project at the National Bank of India, the transfer service dashboard showed exactly this: as traffic rose, the database connection pool saturated to a hundred percent, which simultaneously slowed the successful transfers for customers like Rajesh and Priya, pushing their p99 latency over five hundred milliseconds, and caused a burst of fast-reject errors when no connection was free. Because we kept success and failure latency separate, the fast rejects did not disguise the problem, and because we watched saturation as a leading signal, we could see the pool was the root cause rather than guessing. The principle I always state is that latency and errors are my primary user-facing signals, traffic gives context, and saturation warns me before things break — and alerting on these four at the user-facing level, with the deeper resource metrics kept for diagnosis, is the most efficient way to know a service's true health.
